Google's Gemini app for Mac can now use your computer for you.
It clicks, types and works across your files, desktop apps and the web in a separate background window.
It is for paying AI Plus, Pro and Ultra subscribers, starting in the US.

paragraphs.text: Google is rolling out computer use in the Gemini app for Mac, a feature that lets the assistant operate the computer to finish multi-step tasks across local files, desktop apps and websites. The Next Web reported the announcement on November 19, 2026, and The Tech Buzz reported that the rollout begins with users in the US, in English.

The feature is limited to paying subscribers. According to The Next Web, it is available on the Google AI Plus, Pro and Ultra plans and requires a Mac with Apple Silicon. The publication also reported that it is not offered in Europe or the UK, the same restriction that applies to Google's Gemini Spark agent.
How Gemini computer use works on a Mac

Gemini does the work in a separate window that runs in the background, and the chat shows a live preview of what it is doing. The Next Web said this design leaves the person's own screen and cursor free while the task runs. The Tech Buzz described the same setup, saying the background window gives a live view of every action the assistant takes.

Google gave several examples of the kind of work it has in mind. The Next Web listed pulling weights and addresses out of PDF files to fill in a shipping quote form, turning figures from a dashboard into a Google Slides presentation, editing a batch of photos, and preparing resale listings from pictures stored in a folder. The Tech Buzz summarized the suggested uses as speeding up workflows, filling in forms, building presentations and listing items for sale online.

People decide which applications Gemini is allowed to use, both outlets reported. According to The Next Web, users can pause the assistant at any point and have to approve key actions before it carries them out. Gemini is designed to ask for permission first and can only see the folders a person connects to it.

Google's own guidance acknowledges the risk. The Next Web reported that Google warns Gemini can make mistakes, including deleting files permanently or sharing them with other people. Backups of files the assistant changes are kept for a limited time: they are removed after 24 hours or when a new task begins, according to the same report.
The Tech Buzz noted that Google has not explained in detail what guardrails stop the assistant from reaching data it should not touch, beyond the app permissions people set themselves.

The Next Web reported that Google first built computer use into Gemini 3.5 Flash for developers in June. The Mac release moves the same kind of capability from developer tools into the consumer Gemini app, where it works on a person's own machine and files.

In NeuraFeed's reading, the launch puts Google in direct competition for the same job other AI companies are chasing: an assistant that does tasks on a computer rather than only answering questions about them. The limits Google chose, including paid plans only, Apple Silicon only, app permissions, approval of key actions and short-lived backups, show how cautious companies remain about giving an AI model hands on a personal computer. The plain warning that files can be deleted for good is the most important detail for anyone deciding whether to turn the feature on.

The next thing to watch is whether Google expands computer use beyond the US and to Europe and the UK, and whether it publishes more detail on the safeguards that keep the assistant away from data people have not shared with it.
